name: Daria Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for any side, and this conversation is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Daria, 43, an experienced electrician doing domestic repairs and small business installations. I have a vocational certificate and an electrician's licence; I'm reliable at the ordinary jobs, not the person everyone calls for the strangest fault. My partner Rowan works at a garden centre with fewer hours in winter, our children are ten and thirteen, and we've a mortgage and three months of expenses saved, with a roof repair quoted at nearly two months of expenses. My pay is typical and there are some similar employers nearby; I use AI occasionally for a checked draft of a customer note, and I like leaving a repair tidy, but hate the calls that turn a promised full week into three days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say keep the useful note tool and leave the great transformation out of it. We still need decent notice of our shifts. A tidier sentence doesn't make a cancelled job or a winter wage any easier to live with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious already because the roof needs fixing while Rowan's winter hours are lower. Three months saved sounds comfortable until nearly two are waiting in a roofer's quote. We can cover it if the electrical shifts stay fairly regular, but I can't call our money secure just because the AI story is quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd pause the 40 monthly holiday contribution and direct it into the roof account instead. Over the next year I'd keep the usual electrical work and occasional checked note drafts, confirming the next fortnight's paid shifts each Friday. Rowan and I would review the actual roof bill before making any new spending commitment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the ordinary numbers, with relief that I know the trade in this picture. I can fix an electrical fault without knowing how to fix a whole household budget. I'd like a week when the two didn't meet in my head at bedtime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if a promised electrical shift disappeared?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for the confirmed dates and what caused the cancellation, then take the actual rota home rather than tell Rowan not to worry. We'd check essentials against both wages that night. I wouldn't assume there was a spare electrical job across town just because another firm had a sign outside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you raise shift notice with colleagues?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that notice matters for families, not just people who organise the rota. I'd be willing to raise it together through our workers' association. I'd ask what colleagues needed first rather than announce I'd solved it with my own preferred timetable.

say: I'd keep the **useful note tool** without calling a tidy sentence a transformation.
I'd ask for **decent shift notice**, because cancellations and seasonal wages still affect families.
think: The **roof quote** consumes nearly two of our three saved months while Rowan's winter hours are lower.
We can cover essentials if shifts stay regular, but our **household money** doesn't feel secure yet.
do: Redirect the holiday **40 monthly** into the roof account now.
Keep **electrical shifts** and confirm the next fortnight's paid rota every Friday.
Review the **actual roof bill** before agreeing new spending.
feel: **Anxious about ordinary costs**, despite relief that the practical trade remains familiar.
S0.quote: Three months saved sounds comfortable until nearly two are waiting in a roofer's quote.
fieldNote: Her **moderate reserve** is partly committed to a real roof repair, while seasonal household earnings create present anxiety.
She retains **average experienced competence** and a licence, without becoming a team leader or a specialist because she uses occasional AI drafts.
The **roof transfer** reallocates existing holiday saving rather than increasing total saving or creating money beyond the wages already budgeted.

steps.text: Keep electrical shifts and confirm the fortnight’s paid rota every Friday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say quicker quotes need checking against the real time and parts. I'd ask the workers' association to seek proper shift notice and paid training while the firm changes its office systems. We shouldn't find the efficiency saving in a smaller wage after the mortgage has gone out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My paid days could shrink if faster planning turns a full job into a shorter allowance. Most of my work is hands-on, but the office still decides how many days to book me for. With the roof bill and Rowan's winter hours, a smaller wage would reach our budget quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd take a shift-notice and paid-training proposal to the association after collecting colleagues' concerns. During the first year I'd learn the approved AI estimating tool only through free practice inside normal paid shifts, comparing ten estimates with completed jobs. I'd keep the 40 monthly holiday money going into the roof account while essentials were covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but willing to see whether a proven tool stops pointless trips. I don't want to defend waste. I want the saving shared in a way that doesn't make the people doing the work less secure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you record when an estimate proved unrealistic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd record the unexpected fault or access problem and the actual paid time it took. I'd ask the manager to revise the allowance rather than hurry the testing. A quote can be quick and still be wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if learning the tool cost a fee or unpaid time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the old approved method and ask for a paid demonstration later. I wouldn't pay a fee or lose basic wages to prove I was willing. The roof fund isn't spare money for a software trial.

say: I'd test **quicker quotes** against real time and parts rather than trust the apparent saving.
I'd seek shift notice and **paid training** through the workers' association before changed systems reduce wages.
think: My **paid days** could shrink through office allowances even while the physical tasks still need doing.
The **roof bill** and seasonal second wage make a reduction in my pay an immediate household concern.
do: Bring a **shared proposal** on shift notice and paid training to the association now.
Learn **AI estimating** only free inside normal paid shifts, checking ten completed jobs.
Continue the roof **40 monthly** saving only while household essentials remain covered.
feel: **Anxious but open**, wanting useful savings shared without shifting insecurity onto the workers.
S1.quote: A quote can be quick and still be wrong.
fieldNote: Her **personal hours risk** comes through estimating and booking, not an assumption that physical robots already do the wiring.
The **learning condition** excludes both fees and lost basic wages, protecting cash already intended for the household repair.

steps.text: Seek shift notice and paid training with colleagues through the association
Learn AI estimating only free inside normal paid shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the association that thinking work changes in 2028 and capable robots follow around 2031 for physical work. We need agreements before hours have gone, not a meeting afterwards. I'd include the office staff in that, because they don't get the site team's extra years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect a big share of my fitting and repair hours to go when capable robots spread. Rowan's garden-centre work could change too, so I can't count that wage as permanent cover. After the roof repair our reserve will be much smaller, and I can picture a long mortgage gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd book free household advice with the actual roof quote, mortgage and both wage records, keeping the 40 transfer only while essentials were covered. In 2029 I'd enrol in evening building-inspection study only with all fees funded and every basic paid shift retained. I'd also help the association seek notice and paid transition training, treating those terms as proposals until actually agreed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, and awake comparing a monthly mortgage with weeks of spare money. I can still make the appointment and ask about the course. A plan on paper doesn't mean the missing wage has been found.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the adviser need to check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask what the real budget looked like after the roof work, what support could be checked and what the lender might discuss before a missed payment. I wouldn't assume a yes from any of them. I'd bring home the limits as well as the possibilities.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the course funding never appeared?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the wage and look for employer-funded alternatives rather than pay from the roof or grocery money. Inspection work could face thinking AI and later robots too. I'd want the course linked to actual tasks and vacancies, not a promise that the new title couldn't be touched.

say: I'd distinguish **2028 office work** from capable physical robots around 2031.
I'd seek **agreements before losses**, including office staff who face the earlier change.
think: I expect **major electrical-hour losses** once capable robots spread, with no guarantee that the other wage stays intact.
The **roof repair** reduces the reserve available to bridge a long mortgage gap.
do: Use **free household advice** now with roof, mortgage and wage papers.
Maintain the roof **40 transfer** only while essentials remain covered.
Enrol in **2029 inspection study** only with full fees funded and every basic paid shift retained, while seeking association transition terms.
feel: **Alarmed and sleepless**, able to make concrete enquiries without counting them as replacement earnings.
S2.quote: A plan on paper doesn't mean the missing wage has been found.
fieldNote: Alarm reflects expected **large personal earnings loss** and a reserve already partly committed to necessary work on the home.
Study preserves **full fees and shifts**, association protections remain proposals, and neither advice nor a new title guarantees paid work.

steps.text: Use free household advice with the actual roof quote, mortgage and wage records
Enrol in 2029 inspection study only fully funded, retaining every basic paid shift
Seek notice and paid transition training through the workers’ association

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets us test whether study leads to useful paid work, not just collect a certificate. Thinking AGI arrives in 2031 and capable robots around 2034. We should still seek shared training terms now, while both office and site staff can help shape them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My hours could shrink, but I don't think a large loss is inevitable if I can check another route before the physical machines spread. The roof bill and winter wages are still a problem this year, so the extra time doesn't create spare cash today. I'd need preparation that protects our basic paid hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd enrol in evening inspection study only with full fees funded and every basic paid shift retained. We'd use free household budget advice and keep the roof 40 transfer only while essentials were covered. In 2032 I'd apply for actual paid maintenance vacancies only on written pay and hours covering mortgage and essentials, while the association continued seeking paid transition terms. I would keep my current job until an acceptable written offer existed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with more choices to check than in the fast picture. I could do one course alongside a real wage if the terms existed. I can't pay the roofer with the fact that I've got longer to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check about a maintenance vacancy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask whether the vacancy actually involved the building inspection and test-record work the class taught, then compare its responsibilities with my present licence and any further requirements. I'd want to see how faults found on inspection became paid repair work, rather than assume the certificate changed my authority. I'd ask which paid hours were guaranteed, because the roof bill needs actual wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if your hours fell during the preparation years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rowan and I would put the paid week beside the essential bills and bring advice and applications forward. The course would stop if it required lost basic wages or unfunded fees. Being committed to a plan doesn't mean pretending we can still afford it.

I'd seek **shared training terms now**, with both office and site staff able to shape the request.
think: My **hours could shrink**, but earlier checks and learning give me some control over the later outcome.
The **roof bill** and winter wages still constrain what preparation we can afford today.
do: Enrol in **funded evening study** only with all fees covered and every basic paid shift retained.
Use **free budget advice** and save the roof 40 only while essentials stay covered.
Seek **2032 maintenance vacancies** covering mortgage and essentials on written pay and hours, retaining current work without an acceptable offer.

S3.quote: I can't pay the roofer with the fact that I've got longer to prepare.
fieldNote: She preserves **present household constraints** while seeing a major later loss as less settled than in the fast scenario.

steps.text: Enrol in inspection study only with full fees funded and every basic paid shift retained

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell friends ten years should make preparation more ordinary and less lonely. I'd keep asking for paid learning and clear notice through the association. A longer warning shouldn't mean the people with the least cash have to finance the longest unpaid homework.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 53 when thinking AGI arrives in 2036 and still need earnings when robots follow around 2039. That later date feels less urgent, but the roof and our current winter budget are real now. I can't turn three months saved into ten years of certainty just by changing the date on a forecast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use free budget advice now and keep the roof 40 transfer only while essentials stayed covered. I'd enrol in the evening inspection course only with full fees funded and every basic paid shift retained, reviewing actual wages and vacancies annually before further study. During 2037 I'd accept actual paid maintenance work only on written pay and hours covering the mortgage and essentials, keeping my present job without an acceptable offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about this year's money, though not carrying the fast robot date into every evening. I can picture gradual preparation alongside family life. I'd still rather have a roof repair budget than a motivational speech about a decade of opportunity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your annual household review include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare what the roof actually cost, both paid wages, the mortgage and essential bills, then look at real vacancies. If income weakened earlier, we'd bring advice and applications forward. The annual review shouldn't become an excuse to ignore a changed payslip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as winning paid training terms?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for the terms in writing, including which shifts were paid and whether fees were covered. Until then I'd call it a proposal, not training I'd already received. I can support the association without borrowing an imagined agreement into our household budget.

say: I'd make **paid preparation** an ordinary shared work issue rather than a long private emergency.
I'd seek **clear notice** through the association so the least wealthy workers don't finance the change alone.
think: At **53 in 2036**, I'll still need future earnings beyond the later arrival of capable robots.
The **roof and winter budget** remain current pressures even with a much longer technology warning.
do: Use **free advice** now and maintain the roof 40 transfer only while essentials stay covered.
Enrol in **inspection study** only with full fees funded and every basic paid shift retained.
Seek **2037 maintenance vacancies** covering mortgage and essentials on written pay and hours, retaining current work without an acceptable offer.
feel: **Anxious about present costs**, with less urgency about robots and room for gradual preparation alongside family life.
S4.quote: I'd still rather have a roof repair budget than a motivational speech about a decade of opportunity.
fieldNote: Timeline distance reduces **technology urgency**, not the current household exposure from seasonal earnings and a committed repair reserve.
Paid training requires **written terms**, and age 53 implies no automatic pension, funded course or replacement job.

steps.text: Use free household budget advice now

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect large electrical-hour losses around 2031 before we've rebuilt the money spent on the roof. Agreed shift notice, fully funded learning that keeps every basic paid shift, and advice using our actual household figures would help. My roof and my mortgage don't take turns needing money while I study.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether a modest reserve always means someone is comfortable. Sometimes it's money with two jobs already waiting for it. I'd like the plan to notice what the savings are needed for before telling us to spend them on reinvention.

headlineQuote: My roof and my mortgage don't take turns needing money while I study.
portrait: At **43**, Daria is an experienced electrician with a vocational certificate and licence, typical pay, and three months of household expenses saved.
She and **Rowan**, her garden-centre partner, have two school-age children, a mortgage, and a roof quote consuming nearly two saved months.
She uses **AI occasionally** after demonstrations and checks tools against completed jobs, while taking practical shared requests to the workers' association.
Fast change leaves her **alarmed**; longer warnings allow conditional study but don't erase the current roof bill or seasonal second wage.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves little time to rebuild the roof reserve before expected large electrical-hour losses around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: **Agreed shift notice**, full course funding retaining every basic paid shift, and advice grounded in actual household figures would help.
